scenario:
Two-player game. It is Player A's turn (their first turn), precombat main phase, stack empty, Player A has priority. Each player has a library of 30 plain filler cards. No other effects affect land plays.

Player A has four Forest cards in hand (call them Forest 1-4).
1. Player A plays Forest 1 as their land play (special action).
2. Player A then tries to play Forest 2.
3. Player A casts Explore. Before casting, two untapped Forests are put onto the battlefield under Player A's control (not via a land play, just placed there) and used to pay {1}{G}. Explore resolves (Player A draws a card).
4. Player A casts a second Explore the same way (two more untapped Forests placed onto the battlefield and used to pay). It resolves.
5. Player A then tries to play Forest 2, then Forest 3, then Forest 4, in that order, all during the same main phase with the stack empty.

questions.question: In step 2 (after playing Forest 1, before any Explore), is Player A allowed to play Forest 2?
In step 5, is Player A allowed to play Forest 2?
In step 5, after Forest 2, is Player A allowed to play Forest 3?
In step 5, after Forests 2 and 3, is Player A allowed to play Forest 4?
After all the attempts in step 5, how many lands has Player A played this turn (counting only land plays, not lands put onto the battlefield otherwise)?

answers.reasoning: With no Explore resolved yet, Player A can play 1 land this turn and has already played 1 (Forest 1). Under 305.2a the play is legal only if the number of lands they can play is greater than the number already played. 1 is not greater than 1, so 305.2b forbids it.

The two resolved Explores each give one additional land play, and the effects add together (Explore ruling: multiple Explores in a turn are cumulative). So Player A can play 1+2=3 lands this turn. The Forests placed directly onto the battlefield were not land plays, so they don't count (305.2a counts only lands played). Only Forest 1 has been played and the step 2 attempt failed, so 3 > 1 and the play is legal. Main phase, empty stack and Player A's own turn are all satisfied (505.6b, 116.2a).
Player A has now played 2 lands (Forests 1 and 2) and can play 3 this turn. 3 > 2, so the play is legal.
Player A has now played 3 lands and can play 3. Under 305.2b they can't play another when the number they can play is equal to or less than the number already played.
The three legal land plays were Forest 1, Forest 2 (step 5) and Forest 3. The Forests put onto the battlefield for mana were not land plays, and the failed attempts don't count.

judge.scenario_issues: The situation doesn't say whether Explore's 'you may' is used. I assumed Player A takes each additional land play. The Forests placed directly onto the battlefield are a test setup step; I assumed they don't count as land plays, as the situation says.

Setting up the starting plane (901.5, 103.7) only turns the top card face up inside the command zone. So the one face-up plane and the two planes in the planar deck are all in the command zone: 3.
The planar deck is kept separately in the command zone (901.3, 901.4). Plane cards are never shuffled into or placed in the library, so no plane card is in Player A's library.

The same rules apply to a plane that is still in the planar deck. 901.4 and 311.2 say plane cards stay in the command zone 'both while they're part of a planar deck and while they're face up', and 400.4b keeps them there. The targeted card stays in the command zone, still in the planar deck.

To planeswalk, the face-up plane goes face down on the bottom of its owner's planar deck, and the top card of the planar deck is turned face up (701.31b, 901.11). Both actions happen inside the command zone. Steps 1-2 moved nothing (311.2, 400.4b). So Krosa, Goldmeadow and Tazeem are all still in the command zone: 3.

scenario: This concerns the game setup for a Conspiracy Draft game (casual variant, CR 905), after the draft is done, using the variant's default multiplayer setup and no extra options. No cards are involved. Two group sizes are checked: (1) whether the Conspiracy Draft default setup is a valid game configuration for exactly 2 players, and for exactly 4 players; (2) which multiplayer options the default setup uses. Then a Conspiracy Draft game with that default setup starts with four players, Player A, Player B, Player C and Player D, and we ask how the players relate to each other.

questions.question: Is the Conspiracy Draft default game setup valid for a game of exactly 2 players?
Is the Conspiracy Draft default game setup valid for a game of exactly 4 players?
Does the default Conspiracy Draft setup use the 'attack multiple players' option?
Does the default Conspiracy Draft setup use the limited range of influence option?
In the four-player Conspiracy Draft game, which of Players B, C and D are opponents of Player A?

answers.reasoning: 905.3 says a Conspiracy Draft game is a multiplayer game, and its default setup is the Free-for-All variant. A multiplayer game is one that begins with more than two players (100.1b, 800.1). A game that begins with exactly two players is a two-player game (100.1a), so the multiplayer Free-for-All default setup isn't a valid configuration for it. In casual play people do run 2-player Conspiracy games, but going by the rule text the answer is no.
Four players is more than two, so this is a multiplayer game (100.1b, 800.1). That makes the Free-for-All default setup in 905.3 / 806 valid.
905.3 names the attack multiple players option explicitly. That option also meets 806.2b, which requires exactly one of attack left, attack right or attack multiple players.
905.3 says the default setup is 'without the limited range of influence option'. This matches 806.2a.

In Free-for-All, players compete as individuals against each other (806.1), so there are no teams. The glossary defines an opponent as someone a player is playing against (102.2, 102.3). Without limited range of influence, every other player is an opponent of Player A.

ambiguities.why: The CR never says outright that a 2-player Conspiracy Draft game is forbidden. The answer rests on 905.3 calling it a multiplayer game and on 100.1b defining multiplayer as more than two players. Someone could read the 2-player case as permitted with the multiplayer options simply doing nothing.

judge.scenario_issues: The situation doesn't give the seating order or any team arrangement. I assumed default Free-for-All with no teams.

scenario:
Two-player game (Player A and Player B). Each of the two scenarios below is a separate, fresh game. In both, it is Player A's first turn, precombat main phase, and Player A has priority. No other permanents are relevant.

The only relevant object is a custom test creature, "One Three": a vanilla creature card (creature type only, no subtypes, colorless, no mana cost, no abilities) with printed power/toughness 1/3. It is owned and controlled by Player A and is on the battlefield, untapped, with no counters.

Each "effect" below is a custom colorless instant with mana cost {0} that Player A casts from hand targeting One Three; it resolves fully (both players pass) before the next one is cast. Each instant's text is the stated effect "until end of turn". The turn does not advance in either scenario.

Scenario 1:
1. Player A casts and resolves "Target creature gets +0/+1 until end of turn" targeting One Three.
2. Player A casts and resolves "Switch target creature's power and toughness until end of turn" targeting One Three. (Checkpoint 1: the creature's power/toughness is observed here.)
3. Player A casts and resolves "Target creature gets +5/+0 until end of turn" targeting One Three. (Checkpoint 2: power/toughness observed here.)

Scenario 2 (new game, same starting setup):
1. Player A casts and resolves "Target creature gets +0/+1 until end of turn" targeting One Three.
2. Player A casts and resolves "Switch target creature's power and toughness until end of turn" targeting One Three.
3. Player A casts and resolves another "Switch target creature's power and toughness until end of turn" targeting One Three. (Checkpoint 3: power/toughness observed here.)

questions.question: Scenario 1, Checkpoint 1: what are One Three's power and toughness?
Scenario 1, Checkpoint 2: what are One Three's power and toughness?
Scenario 2, Checkpoint 3: what are One Three's power and toughness?

answers.reasoning: Base 1/3. Layer 7c applies the +0/+1, giving 1/4. Layer 7d then applies the switch, giving 4/1.

Sublayers apply in order no matter when each effect was created. All 7c modifications go before the 7d switch, even the +5/+0 created after it (613.4 orders by sublayer first; timestamp order only applies within a sublayer). So: 1/3 base, then +0/+1 and +5/+0 in 7c give 6/4, then the switch in 7d gives 4/6.
Base 1/3, plus +0/+1 in 7c, gives 1/4. Layer 7d applies both switch effects in timestamp order. The first gives 4/1 and the second swaps it back to 1/4.

judge.scenario_issues: None. The scenario says the turn does not advance, so all until-end-of-turn effects stay active at each checkpoint.

scenario:
Two-player game. It is Player A's first turn, precombat main phase. Both players are at 20 life. No planeswalkers are on the battlefield.

Battlefield: Player A controls an untapped Mountain and an untapped Plains. Player B controls four untapped Islands and a Grizzly Bears (2/2, no damage).

1. Player A casts Boros Charm (from hand), choosing the first mode ("Boros Charm deals 4 damage to target player or planeswalker") and targeting Player B, paying {R}{W} with the Mountain and Plains.
2. In response, Player B casts Deflection (from hand, paying {3}{U} with the four Islands), targeting Boros Charm on the stack.
3. Deflection resolves. Player B is asked to choose the new target for Boros Charm. Player B tries to pick Grizzly Bears as the new target (hoping to redirect it to a creature, which only the charm's double-strike mode could target); if that choice isn't allowed, Player B takes whatever the game requires instead.
4. Afterwards, Boros Charm resolves.

questions.question: When Deflection resolves, is Grizzly Bears a legal choice for Boros Charm's new target?
When Deflection resolves, is Player A a legal choice for Boros Charm's new target?
After Deflection resolves, which mode of Boros Charm is chosen? Answer with the mode's position in the list (1 = damage, 2 = indestructible, 3 = double strike).
After Boros Charm resolves, what is Player A's life total?
After Boros Charm resolves, what is Player B's life total?
After Boros Charm resolves, how much damage is marked on Grizzly Bears?

answers.reasoning: Boros Charm was cast with mode 1 (target player or planeswalker). Changing a target can't change the mode (700.2f), and under 115.7a the new target must be a legal target for the spell as it is, meaning a player or planeswalker. A creature is not a legal target for mode 1.

Mode 1 can target any player. Player A is a legal target and is different from the current target, Player B. With no planeswalkers on the battlefield, Player A is the only other legal target, so Deflection changes the target to Player A. Deflection's ruling says the target stays the same only when no other legal target exists.
The mode is chosen at casting (700.2a). Changing the target can't change it (700.2f), so the spell stays in mode 1.
The target was changed to Player A, who is still a legal target when the spell resolves (608.2b). Boros Charm deals 4 damage to Player A, so 20 - 4 = 16.
Player B is no longer the target, so Player B takes no damage.
Grizzly Bears could not become the target and mode 1 deals damage only to its target, so no damage is marked on it.

judge.scenario_issues: "Takes whatever the game requires instead" is read to mean that Deflection's change must go to another legal target. With no planeswalkers on the battlefield, Player A is the only option (115.7a; Deflection ruling: "If there is no other legal target for the spell, this does not change the target."). I assumed nothing prevents Player A from being targeted, such as hexproof or shroud. If Player B could instead decline the change and keep Player B as the target, the answers to q4 and q5 would become 20 and 16.

scenario:
Two-player game, Player A and Player B. It is Player A's turn 1, precombat main phase; Player A has priority with an empty stack. All custom objects below have mana cost {0} and no other characteristics than those listed.

Custom test objects:
- "Watcher A" and "Watcher B": each is a 1/1 colorless creature card (no creature subtypes), owned by Player B, with the single ability "Whenever another creature enters, you gain 1 life." Both start on the battlefield under Player B's control.
- Two copies of a custom "Banisher Priest": a 2/2 white creature with mana cost {0} and the ability "When this creature enters, exile target creature an opponent controls until this creature leaves the battlefield." Owned by Player A.

Actions, in order:
1. Player A casts the first Banisher Priest from hand (cost {0}). It resolves and enters the battlefield under Player A's control. Its enters trigger goes on the stack targeting Watcher A. (Any other triggered abilities that trigger here are put on the stack and resolve as normal.) Everything on the stack resolves; Watcher A is exiled until the first Priest leaves the battlefield.
2. Player A casts the second Banisher Priest from hand. It resolves and enters; its enters trigger targets Watcher B. Everything on the stack resolves (including any other triggers); Watcher B is exiled until the second Priest leaves the battlefield. Both Watchers are now in exile.
3. Call Player B's life total at this moment L.
4. A single effect then destroys both Banisher Priests simultaneously (they go to Player A's graveyard at the same time). Afterwards, players keep passing priority until the stack is empty, letting every resulting triggered ability resolve.

questions.question: After everything resolves, in which zone is Watcher A?
questions.answer_format: one zone: battlefield, graveyard, exile, hand, library, stack or command

questions.question: After everything resolves, in which zone is Watcher B?
questions.answer_format: one zone: battlefield, graveyard, exile, hand, library, stack or command

questions.question: After everything resolves, what is Player B's life total minus L (the net change since step 3)?

answers.reasoning: Watcher A was exiled until the first Priest leaves the battlefield. Destroying that Priest is the specified event, so a second one-shot effect returns Watcher A to the battlefield under its owner's control, which is Player B (610.3, 610.3c).

The same applies to Watcher B and the second Priest. Both Priests leave at the same time, so the two return effects happen at the same time and both Watchers come back in one event (610.3, 610.3c, 610.3d).

The two return effects happen at the same time (610.3d), so both Watchers enter the battlefield together. Every permanent on the battlefield, including the newcomers, is checked for enters triggers (603.6a). Each Watcher sees the other creature enter, but not itself ('another'). That makes two triggers, so Player B gains 1 + 1 = 2. If the returns were one after the other, the first Watcher to return would see the second, giving 1 life plus the second Watcher's own trigger; the total would also be 2 in that case. The Priests going to the graveyard trigger nothing, because the Watchers are in exile at that moment and have no leaves-the-battlefield abilities. All the earlier life gain (2 in step 1 and 1 in step 2) happened before L was recorded, so it doesn't count.

judge.scenario_issues: Nothing important is missing. I assumed that no other effects change the life total or the zone changes, and that each Priest's enters ability resolved and exiled its target as described. The Watchers' "another creature enters" triggers in steps 1 and 2 happen before L is recorded, so they don't affect the answers.

Immediately after Delay resolves, how many instances of the suspend keyword does the Rift Bolt card have?
After Player B's next upkeep (all upkeep triggers resolved), how many time counters are on the exiled Rift Bolt card?

answers.reasoning: Delay counters Rift Bolt, and its replacement effect exiles the card instead of putting it into the graveyard. Under 614.6 the graveyard move never happens and the exile happens in its place. Rift Bolt was still a legal target, so it was countered 'this way'.

Delay exiles the countered card with three time counters on it. The card's own Suspend 1 number doesn't matter here: Rift Bolt wasn't exiled through its suspend static ability, so it gets Delay's three counters.

Rift Bolt already has suspend (Suspend 1—{R}), so Delay's 'If it doesn't have suspend, it gains suspend' does nothing. The card keeps its single printed instance and is suspended, because it is in exile, has suspend and has time counters.

Suspend's upkeep trigger works only in its owner's upkeep. Player B's current turn is already past upkeep, and Player A's upkeep doesn't trigger it. At Player B's next upkeep it triggers once and removes one time counter, so 3 becomes 2. That isn't the last counter, so the cast trigger doesn't happen.

judge.scenario_issues: None that change the answers. I assumed nothing else adds or removes time counters, and that no other upkeep triggers affect Rift Bolt.

scenario:

Setup (identical in both scenarios below):

scenario:

scenario:

Battlefield:

- Mind Control (an Aura), owned by Player C but controlled by Player B (it entered the battlefield under Player B's control). It is attached to Player D's Grizzly Bears. Its static ability gives Player B control of the Grizzly Bears.

The second step ends the control-changing effect that gave B control of it. By the third step, the exile of anything B still controls, the Bears is no longer controlled by B, so it isn't exiled. 800.4a ends Mind Control's effect giving B control of the Bears. Mind Control's ability would stop applying anyway once Mind Control is exiled. With no control-changing effect left, the Bears goes back to its default controller, its owner Player D, who is still in the game. Mind Control is owned by C, but its controller is B, not C, and the effect gives control to 'you', meaning the Aura's controller. So C never gains control of the Bears.

B controls it because it entered under B's control, not through a control-changing effect, so ending such effects doesn't change who controls it. B still controls it at the final step of 800.4a, so it is exiled right away. This isn't a state-based action. The Aura doesn't go to C's graveyard.

I assumed B controls it by default as the player who put it onto the battlefield, and that no control-changing effect is involved. If an effect had given B control, it would end under 800.4a and C would get Mind Control back. In that case Mind Control would stay on the battlefield, and C would gain control of the Bears.

Each player's library is 30 identical vanilla test cards named "Filler", custom objects with no types, no mana cost and no rules text (traditional Magic cards for the purposes of the rules). A Magic subgame is started, as when Shahrazad resolves (Shahrazad itself is not in play; the subgame starts directly). Each player's whole main-game library becomes their deck for the subgame. The subgame goes through its normal start: a random player goes first, each player shuffles and draws a 7-card opening hand, and nobody mulligans. Then, in the subgame, during Player A's precombat main phase:
1. An effect exiles one Filler card from Player A's subgame hand. It goes to the subgame's exile zone.
2. Another Filler card from Player A's subgame hand is put onto the subgame battlefield under Player A's control. That permanent then phases out.

The subgame then ends with these cards still in place: one in the subgame exile, one phased out on the subgame battlefield, and the rest in Player A's subgame hand and library. Each player's other cards are in their own subgame hand and library. Play returns to the main game.

questions.question: After the subgame ends, how many cards are in Player A's main-game library?
After the subgame ends, is any object from the subgame (including the phased-out Filler) on the main game's battlefield?
After the subgame ends, how many cards are in the main game's exile zone?

answers.reasoning: Under 729.2, Player A's 30 main-game library cards became their subgame library. Under 729.5, when the subgame ends, each player takes every traditional card they own that is in the subgame (anything outside the subgame command zone), puts it into their main-game library and shuffles. The rule says this explicitly includes cards in the subgame exile zone and cards that represent phased-out permanents. So the exiled Filler, the phased-out Filler, and every Filler in A's subgame hand and library all go back. Nothing left the subgame for another zone, so A's main-game library holds 30 cards again. The Shahrazad ruling about exile agrees.

Under 729.5, cards on the subgame battlefield, including ones that represent phased-out permanents, go to their owner's main-game library. Every other subgame object stops existing, along with the subgame's zones. Under 729.1b, nothing from the subgame has any meaning in the main game unless the creating effect says so. The main-game battlefield was empty and nothing put a subgame object onto it.

The main-game exile zone was empty. The card exiled during the subgame went to the subgame's own exile zone, which is a separate zone (729.2). Under 729.5, cards in the subgame exile go to the owner's main-game library, and the subgame zones then stop existing. Nothing is put into the main-game exile.

That affects only Shahrazad's life loss, which none of the questions ask about (and Shahrazad isn't actually resolving here). scenario:
Two-player game. It is Player A's first turn, precombat main phase, Player A has priority, and the stack is empty. No mana is in anyone's mana pool.

Scenario 1:
- Player A controls "Blue Payer", a custom creature (test object, no mana cost, no creature types worth mentioning; colorless) with base power/toughness 3/4. It has no summoning sickness concerns (its ability has no {T} in the cost). Its text is:
  1. "{R}: This creature gets +1/+0 until end of turn."
  2. "You may spend blue mana as though it were mana of any color to pay the activation costs of this creature's abilities."
- Player B controls "Green Tax", a custom enchantment (test object) with the static ability: "Activated abilities of creatures cost {G} more to activate." (applies to abilities of creatures controlled by any player).
- Player A controls two untapped basic Islands and no other mana sources (no other lands or permanents).
Player A attempts to activate Blue Payer's "{R}: +1/+0" ability, paying the mana using their Islands (tapping lands for mana as needed). If the activation succeeds, both players then pass and the ability resolves.

Scenario 2 (a separate fresh game, same turn/step setup):
- Player A controls "Plain Pumper", a custom creature 3/4 with only the ability "{R}: You gain 1 life." It has no ability that lets mana be spent as though it were another color.
- Player A controls two untapped basic Islands and no other mana sources. No "Green Tax" or other cost-modifying effects are present.
Player A attempts to activate Plain Pumper's "{R}" ability.

questions.question: In Scenario 1, can Player A legally activate Blue Payer's {R} ability (with Green Tax on the battlefield) paying only with mana from the two Islands?
In Scenario 1, after the activation is attempted, how many of Player A's two Islands are tapped?
In Scenario 1, after the ability resolves, what is Blue Payer's power/toughness?
In Scenario 2, can Player A legally activate Plain Pumper's {R} ability using only the two Islands?

answers.reasoning: Under 601.2f (which 602.2b applies to activation), the total cost is the {R} activation cost plus Green Tax's {G} increase, so {R}{G}. 602.1e says an effect that changes how a player may pay an ability's 'activation cost' applies to the total cost, increases included. Blue Payer's 'spend blue mana as though it were mana of any color' therefore covers both {R} and {G}. By 609.4b this changes only how the cost may be paid, not the cost itself, so two {U} from the Islands pay {R}{G}.
The total cost {R}{G} needs two mana, so both Islands are tapped for {U}{U} and that mana is spent (601.2g-h, 605.3).
The ability resolves and gives +1/+0 until end of turn: base 3/4 becomes 4/4.

With no effect that lets mana be spent as another color, the {R} cost needs red mana. The Islands make only {U}, so the cost can't be paid (601.2h: unpayable costs can't be paid), and the activation is illegal and rewound.

judge.scenario_issues: Scenario 1 says Player A only "attempts" the activation, so q2 depends on whether it succeeds. Under 602.1e it succeeds, so both Islands are tapped. Scenario 2 doesn't ask how many Islands end up tapped. If the engine taps Islands before failing, the activation should be rewound (CR 732-style reversal / 602.2 illegal-action rule). I assumed Green Tax's "cost {G} more" is a cost increase that adds {G} to the total cost.

scenario:
Two-player game. It is Player A's first turn, precombat main phase, and Player A has priority. Every library holds only filler cards that play no part here.

Scenario 1:
- Player B controls a Hill Giant (3/3) on the battlefield. It is untapped and has no counters.
- Player A has a Matter Reshaper (3/2 colorless Eldrazi creature card) in hand. Player A controls untapped basic Wastes lands that produce exactly the {3} needed for Titan's Presence.
- Player A casts Titan's Presence and targets Player B's Hill Giant. To pay the additional cost, Player A reveals Matter Reshaper from their hand and pays {3} by tapping the Wastes.
- While Titan's Presence is on the stack, an effect discards Matter Reshaper: it moves from Player A's hand to Player A's graveyard. No other spells or abilities are cast or activated.
- Titan's Presence resolves.

Scenario 2 (a separate, fresh game with the same starting setup):
- Player B controls a Grizzly Bears (2/2) on the battlefield.
- Player A again has Matter Reshaper in hand and enough Wastes to pay {3}.
- Player A casts Titan's Presence, targets the Grizzly Bears and reveals Matter Reshaper from hand for the additional cost.
- Matter Reshaper stays in Player A's hand. Nobody casts or activates anything in response, and Titan's Presence resolves.

questions.question: Scenario 1: right after Titan's Presence is cast, while it is still on the stack and before Matter Reshaper is discarded, is Matter Reshaper revealed?
Scenario 1: after Titan's Presence resolves, is Hill Giant still on the battlefield?
Scenario 2: while Titan's Presence is on the stack, is Matter Reshaper in Player A's hand revealed?
Scenario 2: after Titan's Presence has resolved and left the stack, is Matter Reshaper (still in Player A's hand) still revealed?

answers.reasoning: Revealing a card is part of the cost to cast Titan's Presence. Under 701.20a, a card revealed as part of a casting cost stays revealed from the moment the spell is announced until the spell leaves the stack. Titan's Presence is still on the stack at this point, so Matter Reshaper is revealed. 701.20b adds that revealing it does not move it out of the hand.

The spell's effect needs information from a specific object, the revealed card. Under 608.2h, if that object is no longer in the zone it was expected to be in, the effect uses its last known information. The cited ruling says the same thing: if the card has left your hand, use its power as it last existed there. Matter Reshaper's last known power is 3. Hill Giant's power is 3, and 3 <= 3, so Hill Giant is exiled. The target is still legal on resolution (608.2b). Matter Reshaper's death trigger does not apply, because it was discarded from hand and never died.
Under 701.20a, a card revealed as part of a casting cost stays revealed while the spell is on the stack.

Under 701.20a, the card stays revealed only until the spell leaves the stack. Titan's Presence has resolved and gone to the graveyard, so Matter Reshaper is no longer revealed, even though it is still in the hand. (Grizzly Bears, power 2 <= 3, is exiled.)

judge.scenario_issues: Scenario 1 does not say what effect discards Matter Reshaper. I assumed it is some outside effect that changes nothing else about the situation. Neither scenario says whether Hill Giant or Grizzly Bears has hexproof or protection; I assumed they have neither, so both targets stay legal. The Titan's Presence rulings could not be found by grepping the rulings file for the card name (the file is probably keyed by oracle_id), so I relied on the ruling text given in the task.

scenario:
Two-player game. It is Player A's turn 1, precombat main phase; Player A has priority. Battlefield: Player A controls Sprouting Phytohydra and Grizzly Bears (both untapped, no counters, nothing attached). Player B controls Hill Giant. Player A has Cytoshape in hand and enough lands to pay its cost.

1. Player A casts Cytoshape targeting Player A's Grizzly Bears. Neither player responds and it resolves. On resolution Player A chooses Sprouting Phytohydra (Player A's) as the nonlegendary creature to be copied, so Grizzly Bears becomes a copy of Sprouting Phytohydra until end of turn.
2. Still in Player A's main phase, Player B's Hill Giant deals 1 non-combat damage to the creature that was Grizzly Bears (an effect with Hill Giant as the source; Hill Giant does not attack). Any triggered ability that results is put on the stack and resolves; whenever Player A is asked whether to use a "you may" choice, Player A answers yes. Everything on the stack resolves with no responses.
3. The game then proceeds normally (both players passing priority with nothing else happening) through the rest of Player A's turn, including the end step and cleanup step, until Player B's next turn reaches its upkeep step.

questions.question: Immediately after Cytoshape resolves (step 1), what is the name of the creature that was originally Grizzly Bears?
After step 2 (all triggered abilities resolved), how many tokens named Sprouting Phytohydra does Player A control?
In Player B's upkeep (after step 3), what is the name of the permanent that was originally Grizzly Bears?
In Player B's upkeep (after step 3), what is the name of the token Player A created in step 2?

answers.reasoning: Cytoshape's copy effect makes the target take on the copiable values of the chosen creature (707.2), which include its name. So the former Grizzly Bears is now named Sprouting Phytohydra. It's a 0/2 with defender and the damage trigger. The effect lasts until end of turn (611.2a).

The former Bears now has Sprouting Phytohydra's triggered ability. When Hill Giant deals it 1 damage, the trigger fires once. Player A says yes to the 'you may' and creates one token copy. The 0/2 creature takes 1 damage and survives, so nothing else happens. That leaves 1 token named Sprouting Phytohydra.

In the cleanup step, all 'until end of turn' effects end (514.2), and that includes Cytoshape's copy effect (611.2a). The permanent goes back to its printed characteristics, so it is Grizzly Bears again in Player B's upkeep. The Scryfall ruling says the same: the Cytoshaped creature reverts.

The token copies the copiable values of the object it copied, and other copy effects count toward those values (707.2/707.3). When the token was made, that meant Sprouting Phytohydra's values. They become the token's own copiable values and are not tied to the Cytoshape effect. When the Cytoshape effect ends, the token is unchanged and is still named Sprouting Phytohydra. The ruling confirms this: 'the token copying it will not' revert.

judge.scenario_issues: The scenario doesn't say what mechanism makes Hill Giant deal the 1 non-combat damage. I assumed some generic effect whose source is Hill Giant. The answers don't depend on what that mechanism is.

scenario:
Two-player game, both players at 20 life, each with a library of ordinary filler cards. It is Player A's first turn (Player A is the starting player), precombat main phase, Player A has priority, the stack is empty.

Battlefield at the start:
- Player A controls Grizzly Bears (untapped), which has been under Player A's control continuously since the start of this turn (not summoning sick).
- Player A then puts Llanowar Elves onto the battlefield during this main phase via an effect, so the Elves entered the battlefield this turn (it has not been under Player A's control since the turn began).
Player B controls no relevant permanents.

Actions:
1. In this precombat main phase of turn 1, Player A casts Teferi's Protection (paying {2}{W}); Player B does not respond and it resolves. Teferi's Protection is exiled as part of its resolution.
2. The game proceeds normally: the rest of Player A's turn 1 is played out with no further actions (no attacks), then Player B's turn 2 begins and proceeds to Player B's precombat main phase (no relevant actions by either player).
3. The game continues: Player B's turn 2 ends, and Player A's turn 3 begins with the untap step and proceeds through upkeep and draw to Player A's precombat main phase. No one takes any other actions.
4. In this precombat main phase of turn 3, Player A attempts to activate Llanowar Elves' "{T}: Add {G}." ability.
5. The game then moves to the beginning of combat step of Player A's turn 3, and Player A wants to declare Grizzly Bears as an attacker attacking Player B.

questions.question: Immediately after Teferi's Protection resolves on turn 1, are Grizzly Bears and Llanowar Elves both phased out?
During Player B's precombat main phase on turn 2, are Grizzly Bears and Llanowar Elves both phased out?
During Player A's precombat main phase on turn 3, are Grizzly Bears and Llanowar Elves both phased in (not phased out)?
In step 4, can Player A legally activate Llanowar Elves' {T}: Add {G} ability (adding {G} to Player A's mana pool)?
In step 5, is declaring Grizzly Bears as an attacker attacking Player B a legal attack declaration, and if declared, is Grizzly Bears attacking?

answers.reasoning: When Teferi's Protection resolves, all permanents Player A controls phase out. That includes Grizzly Bears and also Llanowar Elves, even though the Elves entered this turn: the effect covers every permanent A controls, and summoning sickness doesn't matter here. Phasing out turns their status to phased out (702.26b).

Phased-out permanents phase in only during the untap step of the player who controlled them when they phased out (502.1, 702.26a). Player B's turn 2 untap step phases in only permanents that phased out under B's control. So A's Bears and Elves stay phased out through B's turn.

At the start of A's turn 3 untap step, all phased-out permanents that A controlled when they phased out phase in at the same time, before anything untaps (502.1, 702.26a, 702.26c). This happens even though they phased out because of a spell rather than the phasing keyword. Both are phased in by the precombat main phase.

Under 302.6, a {T} ability of a creature can be activated only if A has controlled it continuously since A's most recent turn began. Phasing doesn't change zone or control, and history checks don't treat phasing as leaving or entering A's control (702.26d). The Elves have been under A's control since turn 1, which covers the whole of turn 3. The cited Teferi's Protection ruling confirms it: creatures that phase in as your next untap step begins can pay {T} costs that turn. The Elves are also untapped, so the mana ability can be activated and adds {G}.

Grizzly Bears is phased in and untapped, and A has controlled it continuously since before turn 3 (302.6, 702.26d). The ruling says creatures that phase in during the untap step can attack that turn. Nothing restricts the attack, so declaring it attacking Player B is legal and Bears becomes an attacking creature (508.1). Strictly, attackers are declared in the declare attackers step that follows beginning of combat. I read step 5 as meaning the declaration in that step.

judge.scenario_issues: Step 5 says Player A declares attackers "at the beginning of combat step". Under 508.1, attackers are declared in the declare attackers step, so I assumed it means the declaration made in that step. On turn 3, A's life total can no longer be locked by Teferi's Protection ("until your next turn" ended when turn 3 began), but nothing in the questions depends on that. I assumed Llanowar Elves was untapped when it phased out, so it is untapped on turn 3; the untap step would untap it anyway.

scenario:
Two separate two-player games (Player A and Player B). No combat or casting happens; Auras are put directly onto the battlefield already attached (not cast), one after another, so each later one has a later timestamp. Each Aura is controlled by Player A; the creatures are controlled by Player B.

Game 1:
1. Player B has Grizzly Bears on the battlefield.
2. Player A's Lignify is put onto the battlefield attached to Grizzly Bears.
3. Then Player A's Reprobation is put onto the battlefield attached to the same Grizzly Bears (so Reprobation's timestamp is later than Lignify's).
4. Then Player B gets Karn, Silver Golem on the battlefield, and a second Reprobation controlled by Player A is put onto the battlefield attached to Karn, Silver Golem. Nothing else affects Karn.

Game 2 (a fresh game):
1. Player B has Grizzly Bears on the battlefield.
2. Player A's Reprobation is put onto the battlefield attached to Grizzly Bears.
3. Then Player A's Lignify is put onto the battlefield attached to the same Grizzly Bears (so Lignify's timestamp is later than Reprobation's).

The questions ask about the permanents' characteristics after each of these steps.

questions.question: Game 1: after Lignify and then Reprobation are attached, what are Grizzly Bears' power and toughness?
Game 1: after Lignify and then Reprobation are attached, what creature types does Grizzly Bears have?
Game 1: with Reprobation attached to Karn, Silver Golem, is Karn an artifact?
Game 1: with Reprobation attached to Karn, Silver Golem, is Karn legendary?
Game 2: after Reprobation and then Lignify are attached, what are Grizzly Bears' power and toughness?
Game 2: after Reprobation and then Lignify are attached, what creature types does Grizzly Bears have?

answers.reasoning: Both Auras set base P/T in layer 7b (613.4b). They're applied in timestamp order (613.7), so Lignify's 0/4 goes first and Reprobation's later 0/1 overwrites it. This matches the cited Reprobation ruling.

In layer 4 (613.1d), Lignify first makes the creature a Treefolk, replacing Bear (205.1a). Reprobation, which has the later timestamp, then makes it a Coward creature and removes all other types and creature types (205.1a). So it is only a Coward.

Reprobation sets the card type to creature, and that replaces existing card types (205.1a). Its reminder text says the creature loses all other types. Karn therefore loses the artifact type and is only a creature.
Changing card types or subtypes doesn't change supertypes (205.4b). Reprobation's reminder text also says the creature keeps all supertypes, so Karn is still legendary.
Both effects apply in layer 7b in timestamp order. Lignify is later, so its 0/4 overwrites Reprobation's 0/1. This matches the second sentence of the Reprobation ruling.

In layer 4, Reprobation first makes it a Coward creature. Lignify, which has the later timestamp, then sets its creature type to Treefolk. That replaces Coward (205.1a), and the creature card type stays.

judge.scenario_issues: None. I assumed Reprobation's current Oracle reminder text: it keeps all supertypes but loses all other types and creature types.

scenario:
Two-player game. It is Player A's first turn, precombat main phase; Player A is the active player. Player B controls three untapped creatures on the battlefield, all with no damage marked and no counters: Nomads en-Kor (1/1), Hill Giant (3/3) and Grizzly Bears (2/2). Life totals are 20 each and irrelevant.

1. Player A casts Lightning Bolt (paying {R} from their own land) targeting Nomads en-Kor.
2. While Lightning Bolt is on the stack, Player B activates Nomads en-Kor's {0} ability targeting Hill Giant; that ability resolves (Lightning Bolt still on the stack).
3. Player B activates the ability again, targeting Hill Giant; it resolves.
4. Player B activates the ability a third time, targeting Grizzly Bears; it resolves.
5. Lightning Bolt then resolves (everything on the stack resolves, state-based actions are checked).
6. Later in the same turn (same main phase), Player A casts Shock (paying {R}) targeting Nomads en-Kor; Player B activates nothing further, and Shock resolves, followed by state-based actions.

questions.question: Immediately after Lightning Bolt has resolved (step 5), in which zone is Nomads en-Kor?
questions.answer_format: one zone: battlefield, graveyard, exile, hand, library, stack or command

questions.question: After Lightning Bolt has resolved (step 5), how much damage is marked on Nomads en-Kor?
After Lightning Bolt has resolved (step 5), how much damage is marked on Hill Giant?
After Lightning Bolt has resolved (step 5), how much damage is marked on Grizzly Bears?
After Shock has resolved and state-based actions are checked (step 6), in which zone is the Nomads en-Kor card?

answers.reasoning: Each activation creates its own redirection shield for 'the next 1 damage' (614.9). Player B could activate the {0} ability whenever they had priority, including with Bolt on the stack (117.1b), and the ruling says they can use it as many times as they want before damage is dealt. When Bolt would deal 3 damage to Nomads, Player B, as the affected creature's controller, applies the three shields one at a time (616.1, 616.1f). Each shield moves 1 damage to its target, so all 3 damage is redirected. Nomads has no damage marked, so 704.5g does not destroy it and it stays on the battlefield.
Three 1-damage shields each redirect 1 of Bolt's 3 damage (614.9, 616.1f), so no damage reaches Nomads en-Kor.
Two shields target Hill Giant, so each sends 1 damage to it, for 2 in total. That is less than its toughness of 3, so it survives.
One shield targets Grizzly Bears, so it is dealt 1 damage. That is less than its toughness of 2.

Bolt's damage used up all three shields (each applies only once, 614.5), and no new activation was made. Shock therefore deals 2 damage to Nomads en-Kor, a 1/1. That is lethal damage, so state-based actions destroy it (704.5g) and the card goes to its owner's graveyard.

judge.scenario_issues: None that matter. I assumed none of the creatures is removed or stops being a creature before the redirections happen. Otherwise 614.9 would make the affected shield do nothing.

scenario:
Two-player game. It is Player A's first turn, precombat main phase; Player A has priority and the stack is empty.

Battlefield:
- Player A controls Woe Strider (no counters, untapped, not summoning sick; it was simply put onto the battlefield, so no enters trigger happened and there is no Goat token), plus an untapped Swamp, Swamp and Wastes.
- Player B controls Crook of Condemnation (untapped) and one untapped Wastes, so Player B could activate the Crook's "{1}, {T}: Exile target card from a graveyard" ability whenever Player B has priority.

Player A's graveyard: four Grizzly Bears cards. Player A's hand: Murder.

Actions:
1. Player A casts Murder targeting their own Woe Strider, paying {1}{B}{B} with the two Swamps and the Wastes.
2. Both players pass priority whenever they get it (Player B never activates Crook of Condemnation or does anything else). Murder resolves and destroys Woe Strider, which goes to Player A's graveyard. Play continues until the stack is empty and Woe Strider is in the graveyard and some player holds priority.
3. At that point, five untapped Swamps are put onto the battlefield under Player A's control (so Player A has {B}{B}{B}{B}{B} available).
4. Player A then casts Woe Strider from the graveyard using its escape ability, paying {3}{B}{B} with the five Swamps and exiling the four Grizzly Bears from the graveyard. Both players then pass and everything on the stack resolves.

questions.question: Right after Murder resolves (stack empty, Woe Strider in Player A's graveyard), which player receives priority first?
questions.answer_format: one of: Player A, Player B

questions.question: Between Woe Strider being put into the graveyard and Player A casting it with escape, does Player B ever receive priority (and so get a chance to, e.g., exile it with Crook of Condemnation)?
At that moment (after Player A has the five Swamps), is it legal for Player A to cast Woe Strider from the graveyard using escape?
Immediately after Player A casts Woe Strider with escape, how many objects are on the stack?
After everything resolves, in which zone is Woe Strider?
questions.answer_format: one zone: battlefield, graveyard, exile, hand, library, stack or command

questions.question: After everything resolves, what are Woe Strider's power and toughness?

answers.reasoning: After a spell (not a mana ability) resolves, the active player receives priority (117.3b). It is Player A's turn, so Player A gets priority first. SBAs and triggers are checked before priority is given (117.5), and none apply here.

Woe Strider reaches the graveyard while Murder resolves. After that, Player A (the active player) gets priority (117.3b) and can cast a spell right away. Player B only gets priority if Player A passes (117.3d). The five Swamps are put onto the battlefield as a test setup step, not a game action, so no priority passes happen. Player A casts Woe Strider while still holding that first priority. This matches the cited Woe Strider ruling that you can cast it 'before an opponent can take any actions'.

Escape is a static ability that works while the card is in its owner's graveyard. It lets Player A cast the card from there for its escape cost as an alternative cost (702.138a, 118.9). A creature spell needs sorcery timing: it is Player A's main phase, Player A has priority, and the stack is empty (307.1). The costs can be paid: {3}{B}{B} from five Swamps, and four other cards (the Grizzly Bears) can be exiled.

The only object on the stack is the Woe Strider creature spell. Murder has already resolved. 'Escapes with two +1/+1 counters' is a replacement effect that applies as it enters (702.138c), not a trigger. The Goat trigger happens only after it enters. Mana abilities don't use the stack.
The creature spell resolves and becomes a permanent on the battlefield (608.3). Player B never removes it.

It escaped (702.138b), so it enters with two +1/+1 counters (702.138c): 3/2 base plus 2/2 from the counters = 5/4 (613.4c). The enters trigger only makes a Goat token and doesn't change Woe Strider's stats.

judge.scenario_issues: Step 3 puts the five Swamps onto the battlefield by test setup, not by a game action. I assumed this doesn't pass priority, so Player A still has the priority they got after Murder resolved. On my first pass I didn't see the cited Woe Strider ruling in the rulings file; the grep was by card name, and the file is probably keyed by oracle_id. I read the ruling as quoted in the situation.

scenario: Two-player game. It is Player B's turn, precombat main phase, and Player B has priority. The stack is empty. Player B controls a Plains (a basic land, untapped, on the battlefield since before this turn). Player A controls Imprisoned in the Moon, which was put onto the battlefield already attached to Player B's Plains (it was not cast, so no targeting or casting happened). No other permanents or effects are in play. Player B's mana pool starts empty. With the Aura attached, Player B activates the Plains's only activated ability, a mana ability, by tapping the Plains.

questions.question: While enchanted by Imprisoned in the Moon, does Player B's land still have the land subtype Plains?
While enchanted, how many activated abilities does Player B's land have?
After Player B taps the land for mana, how much colorless mana ({C}) is in Player B's mana pool?
After Player B taps the land for mana, how much white mana ({W}) is in Player B's mana pool?

answers.reasoning: Imprisoned in the Moon makes the permanent a colorless land and removes all other card types. Subtypes are not removed. This is a layer 4 type-changing effect (613.1d). The Plains subtype is a land type, which fits the land card type, so it stays. The cited ruling says this outright: a Plains enchanted this way is still a Plains. The basic supertype also stays (see the ruling on supertypes).

Because the land is still a Plains, rule 305.6 gives it the intrinsic ability '{T}: Add {W}.' In layer 6 (613.1f), Imprisoned in the Moon removes all other abilities, including that intrinsic {W} ability, and grants '{T}: Add {C}.' The ruling confirms the land loses the {W} ability. That leaves one activated ability, '{T}: Add {C}.'
